evaluation.positioning_hook: A rule-following apprentice in a marriage-optimization regime falls for the one woman who makes him feel real, then gets pulled into the system’s inner machinery when he tries to see her again.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean emotional engine and a strong dystopian hook: a young man discovers real feeling inside a system built to manage intimacy. The audience is there, especially for elevated genre buyers, but the concept is more adult and controlled than broad four-quadrant fare.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early in the graduation ritual, the outing app, and the timed date structure. By the time Lewis’s cross-local request escalates to Chance Hunter, the premise is easy to explain in two sentences and the pressure is clear.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Lewis is a solid lead because his obedience, loneliness, and buried defiance are all visible on the page, especially in the restaurant scenes and the interview. Emma and Chance add strong opposing energies, though the supporting cast is more functional than deeply surprising.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s marriage-program world is specific, legible, and unnerving without over-explaining itself. The controlled rituals, app language, and staged intimacy give the piece a confident conceptual identity rather than a generic near-future wrapper.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps escalating from ceremony to outing to cross-local review to the Oregon trip and the interview trap. It moves well, though the middle section leans on repeated date/report beats before the gas-station turn and Chance confrontation sharpen the stakes.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script finds a fresh lane by making romance, surveillance, and social engineering feel inseparable. Lewis’s kiss, the logged reports, and Chance’s reveal that the system wants to scale the moment itself give the premise an immediately ownable logic.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world feels governed by rules, status tiers, app prompts, approvals, and public messaging that all reinforce the same social order. The diner, apartment, mediation room, border convoy, and compound each add a different texture to the same system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is controlled and unnerving, with a clean, clinical surface that keeps cracking open into intimacy and menace. The script has a distinct register in the way it stages silence, ritual, and emotional leakage.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There’s a clear sense that the Union is bigger than Lewis understands, and the Chance Hunter scenes suggest a deeper political machine underneath the romance plot. The ending image and the propaganda montage imply more thematic territory than the plot initially reveals.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Lewis/Emma/Chance triangle is strong and the parents add useful ideological pressure, but this is still fundamentally a lead-driven feature. The supporting relationships are effective rather than especially generative as an ensemble engine.

lead_characters.name: Lewis
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 20s, working-class, likely white; a newly turned-out apprentice in the Union system.
lead_characters.hook: Lewis is a tightly wound young man who has been trained to speak in approved language, follow structure, and suppress instinct, but his body keeps betraying his real feelings. He starts as a model citizen and becomes dangerous precisely because he is sincere; the more he tries to do things correctly, the more obvious it becomes that he wants something the system cannot comfortably contain.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a breakout lead performance like Timothée Chalamet in Call Me by Your Name or Andrew Garfield in Under the Silver Lake — a role that lives in micro-reactions, withheld desire, and the slow collapse of composure. It gives an actor the chance to play repression, awakening, and moral panic in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Emma
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, Northern California local, Union participant with enough confidence to bend the rules without looking rebellious.
lead_characters.hook: Emma is the first person who makes Lewis feel unperformed, and she’s smart enough to understand the danger before he does. She reads as open and grounded, but the script keeps her slightly elusive, which makes her feel like both a romantic possibility and a test of whether authenticity can survive the system.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Zendaya in Malcolm & Marie or Riley Keough in Zola a chance to be magnetic without over-explaining themselves — present-tense, emotionally legible, and quietly disruptive. An actor gets to play warmth, skepticism, and the cost of being the person who sees the trap first.

lead_characters.name: Chance Hunter
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 40s to 50s, Union president and public face of the organization.
lead_characters.hook: Chance is polished, paternal, and disarmingly warm until the mask slides and the coercive logic becomes visible. He’s the kind of antagonist who never needs to raise his voice because he understands that control sounds better when it sounds like care.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is premium villain territory in the vein of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Jeremy Strong in The Trial of the Chicago 7 when he’s weaponizing calm — a role that lets an actor play charm as threat. The appeal is the chance to make ideology feel intimate, seductive, and dangerous.

lead_characters.name: Dana
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 50s, Lewis’s mother, emotionally intuitive but constrained by the family’s belief system.
lead_characters.hook: Dana is the script’s quiet dissenter inside the home: she doesn’t reject the system outright, but she can feel the human cost of its certainty. Her scenes give the story its most grounded emotional counterpoint, because she sees Lewis slipping into performance before he can name it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Patricia Clarkson did in Pieces of April or Laura Linney in The Savages — carry a scene with understatement, moral complexity, and lived-in maternal intelligence. It’s a precision part for someone who can make one kitchen conversation feel like a worldview.

lead_characters.name: Darren
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, Lewis’s father, Union believer and practical traditionalist.
lead_characters.hook: Darren is not a cartoon zealot; he’s a man who genuinely believes structure is kindness and that emotional discipline is the same thing as love. That makes him useful dramatically, because every conversation with Lewis becomes a debate about whether safety is worth the surrender it demands.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor material in the lane of Bryan Cranston in a domestic pressure-cooker or J.K. Simmons when he’s all authority and no apology. The role gives an actor a chance to play conviction without villainizing himself.

lead_characters.name: Shannon
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, Union participant, educated, polished, and highly fluent in the system’s language.
lead_characters.hook: Shannon is Lewis’s first real mirror: she understands the rules, can speak them fluently, and still feels the strain underneath. She’s not a love interest placeholder; she’s a version of the same trapped generation, which makes her scenes quietly revealing about how normalized the system has become.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do controlled, layered work like Jessie Buckley in menacingly polite mode or Elizabeth Olsen in a contained emotional duel. The showcase is in playing someone who sounds compliant while revealing how much she’s managing underneath.

lead_characters.name: Tim R
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s, Union facilitator and mediator trainee supervisor.
lead_characters.hook: Tim R is the bureaucratic face of emotional regulation: calm, procedural, and always one step away from turning private pain into recordable data. He’s important because he makes the system feel institutional rather than merely ideological.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a great role for an actor who can do institutional menace with restraint, in the vein of Michael Stuhlbarg or Shea Whigham when they’re making procedure feel ominous. The appeal is the chance to turn neutrality into threat.

lead_characters.name: Clare
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, married participant in mediation.
lead_characters.hook: Clare is one of the script’s clearest examples of what the Union does to intimacy: she’s trying to speak plainly inside a language designed to flatten conflict. Her discomfort gives the mediation sequence its human ache and makes the system feel invasive rather than abstract.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-rich supporting role that gives an actor a sharp, emotionally contained showcase like Carrie Coon in a domestic argument or Amy Ryan in a procedural pressure scene. The performance opportunity is in making frustration feel civilized until it isn’t.

lead_characters.name: Bob
lead_characters.hook: Bob is the man who has internalized the system so fully that he thinks compliance is the same thing as being a good partner. He’s useful because he shows how the Union’s logic survives not through force alone, but through self-justification.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong supporting role for a grounded character actor in the mold of Paul Sparks or Scoot McNairy — someone who can make passive defensiveness feel specific. The showcase is in playing a man who is both sincere and deeply compromised.

lead_characters.name: Lila
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, Emma’s friend, Northern California local.
lead_characters.hook: Lila is the outside voice in Emma’s world, the one who can say the unsayable without sounding like a manifesto. She gives the coastal scenes a lived-in, less regulated energy and helps define what freedom looks like by contrast.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a lively supporting part in the spirit of a friend role like Beanie Feldstein in Lady Bird — quick, grounded, and emotionally clarifying. It gives an actor room to be funny, skeptical, and affectionate in the same beat.

lead_characters.name: Waitress
lead_characters.hook: The waitress is a small but telling pressure point in the world: she notices the coveralls, the patch, and the social meaning attached to Lewis before he says a word. She helps the script show how status is read instantly in public space.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact, playable role for a character actor who can land a scene with one look and one line, the kind of part that benefits from specificity more than size. It’s a clean showcase for observational realism.

lead_characters.name: Receptionist
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 50s, administrative worker in the Union system.
lead_characters.hook: The receptionist is the face of the machine when the machine is pretending to be neutral. She starts procedural and becomes quietly alarming once Lewis’s request is escalated, which makes her a useful hinge between bureaucracy and power.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do controlled authority like Ann Dowd or Cherry Jones in a system-facing scene. The appeal is the shift from ordinary desk work to a moment of institutional gravity.

lead_characters.name: Guard
lead_characters.hook: The guards are the visible edge of the Union’s enforcement arm: calm, trained, and unbothered by violence. They’re not individualized much, but they are essential to the film’s sense of containment and threat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a functional but effective role for a strong physical performer who can project control without theatricality. The showcase is in stillness, not speech.

lead_characters.name: Waiter
lead_characters.hook: The waiter is another small-world indicator of how scripted the social environment is; even service interactions feel monitored and standardized. He helps reinforce the sense that the Union has colonized ordinary life.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: A clean, scene-specific role for a character actor who can make a procedural beat feel socially loaded. It’s a good one-scene part with texture.

casting_characteristics: Lead requires a young actor who can carry internalized conflict and controlled physicality
No special physical or twin requirements

notable_requirements: border checkpoint and convoy road work

technical.vfx_details: Primarily interface graphics, broadcast screens, signage, and subtle environmental augmentation; no major effects set pieces.
technical.sfx_needs: Single gunshot at the gas station, practical blood effect, convoy movement, and controlled security presence.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical with streaming upside

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the convoy travel, border checkpoint, compound exteriors, and multiple branded environments will push this above a bare-bones indie footprint.

casting.note: Lewis has to carry repression, romantic vulnerability, and eventual ideological fracture; Chance Hunter also needs a very specific blend of warmth and menace to land.

development.note: The script’s strongest turn is the reveal that the system wants to scale Lewis’s experience, and the final propaganda montage pushes the concept into sharper satirical territory than the earlier romance-forward sections.

comp_set.title: Never Let Me Go
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the controlled, melancholy sense of a system shaping intimacy and identity, with romance used as the emotional entry point into a larger social design.

comp_set.title: The Lobster
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the deadpan institutionalization of pairing and the way romance becomes a bureaucratic process with absurdly high emotional stakes.

comp_set.title: Ex Machina
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the sleek, unsettling near-future control language and the sense that a private emotional encounter is actually a test inside a larger system.

comp_set.title: The Handmaid's Tale
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the authoritarian social order, the surveillance of private life, and the political undertow beneath a personal relationship story.

comp_set.title: Her
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the loneliness, curated intimacy, and emotional dependence on a system that promises connection while shaping it.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to elevated speculative thrillers with a strong romantic and political undercurrent.
audience_target.demographics: Skews 25-54, slightly female-leaning but not exclusively; strong appeal to prestige-drama and genre audiences with higher-than-average tolerance for slow-burn worldbuilding.

budget_tier.note: Mostly contemporary interiors with a handful of road, compound, and broadcast set pieces; the convoy and night work add scope but not tentpole scale.

lane_fit.detail: The script sits in the lane where concept clarity, social unease, and actor-forward roles matter more than spectacle. It’s built for buyers who want a smart, commercially legible thriller with enough thematic bite to travel beyond genre-only audiences.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the world is specific and expandable in theory, but no secondary character or distinct universe vector is developed enough to justify franchise planning.

strengths.what_it_means: That clarity makes the script easy to pitch, easy to market, and easy for a buyer to understand as a contained commercial proposition. It gives streamer and indie buyers a fast read on audience, tone, and stakes without needing a long explanation.
strengths.evidence: The graduation ritual, the outing app, the timed date, and the cross-local escalation all establish the engine within the first act.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Lewis is a strong actor magnet.
strengths.what_it_means: The role offers a clean showcase for a young lead who can play repression, longing, and moral awakening without ever becoming broad. That is exactly the kind of part that can elevate a package and attract actor-driven financing or a breakout casting conversation.
strengths.evidence: His body language in the ceremony, the restaurant report scenes, and the gas-station breakdown all track a visible internal fracture.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world has rules that generate story.
strengths.what_it_means: The app, the reporting language, the pair-bond hierarchy, and the cross-local approval process create a system that can keep producing pressure without feeling arbitrary. Buyers respond to worlds that feel operational, because they imply both control and conflict.
strengths.evidence: The outing timer, the emotional-alignment scores, the mediation session, and the executive review with Chance Hunter all deepen the same logic.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The romance is also a political trap.
strengths.what_it_means: That duality gives the movie a sharper commercial identity than a standard dystopian love story, because the emotional payoff and the thriller mechanics are fused. It’s the kind of hook that can pull in both prestige-drama audiences and elevated-genre buyers.
strengths.evidence: Lewis and Emma’s kiss becomes a violation, then a data point, then a lever for Chance’s interview plan.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Chance Hunter is a premium antagonist.
strengths.what_it_means: He gives the project a face for ideology, which is crucial for marketing and for giving the second half a human pressure source. A charismatic institutional villain is a major packaging asset because it creates trailer moments and actor interest.
strengths.evidence: His compound introduction, the warm handshake, and the pivot from reassurance to coercion in the interview scene.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending reframes the whole movie.
strengths.what_it_means: The propaganda montage and final domestic image turn the story from a simple escape narrative into something more unsettling and commercially distinctive. That kind of ending can make a buyer feel the script has thematic ambition beyond the premise.
strengths.evidence: The televised interview, the book cover, the wedding broadcast, and the final blinking red light in the home.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, high-concept elevated thriller with a strong lead role, a marketable romance engine, and a world that feels engineered rather than decorative. It’s the kind of indie-scale package that can attract actor interest, travel on concept alone, and still leave room for thematic bite and a memorable antagonist.

items.area: The middle section repeats the same date logic.
items.detail: The outing/report rhythm is effective, but several restaurant scenes and montage beats cover similar emotional ground before the story pivots into the Oregon trip. That creates a small momentum drag in the center of the feature, even though the worldbuilding remains clear.

items.area: Emma is vivid but still slightly underused.
items.detail: She makes a strong impression in the cross-local date and the phone call, but the script keeps her more as a catalyst than a fully independent force. For buyers, that means the movie still lives or dies primarily on Lewis and Chance rather than on a broader two-hander dynamic.

items.area: The final propaganda turn is a tonal escalation.
items.detail: The interview montage, book cover, wedding broadcast, and final domestic tableau push the piece into overt satirical territory after a more restrained thriller build. That’s a compelling swing, but it is also the point where some buyers will ask whether the movie is primarily a romance, a political thriller, or a dystopian satire.

items.area: The Union’s mechanics stay intentionally opaque.
items.detail: The script smartly withholds some institutional detail, but the buyer will notice that the system’s full legal and social architecture is only partially defined. That’s fine for mood, but it means the concept is strongest as a character-led thriller rather than as a fully mapped world franchise.

items.area: The gas-station shooting is a hard tonal line.
items.detail: The owner’s death is the script’s clearest violence spike, and it arrives in a sequence that is otherwise about procedural travel and ideological pressure. It’s effective, but it will be a conversation point for buyers calibrating audience comfort and the film’s overall rating posture.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is structural, not conceptual: the center repeats the same controlled-date pattern a few times before the story opens up into the Oregon confrontation. Buyers will also clock the tonal jump into overt propaganda satire at the end, which is exciting but makes the film’s lane feel slightly broader than the first half suggests.
